```sql
-- PostgreSQL, table "users"
BEGIN;

ALTER TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS first_name text,
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS last_name  text;

UPDATE users
SET first_name = split_part(btrim(full_name), ' ', 1),
    last_name  = NULLIF(btrim(substr(btrim(full_name),
                   length(split_part(btrim(full_name), ' ', 1)) + 1)), '')
WHERE full_name IS NOT NULL
  AND first_name IS NULL
  AND last_name IS NULL;

COMMIT;
```

I have not run this; it assumes PostgreSQL and a table named `users`. A second run is a no-op because the columns are added with `IF NOT EXISTS` and the backfill only touches rows where both new columns are still NULL, so later edits are not overwritten.

It splits on the first space, so "Mary Ann Smith" becomes "Mary" / "Ann Smith", and a single-word name gets a NULL `last_name`.

I left out dropping `full_name`, which is irreversible; do it in a later migration once the application no longer reads or writes it. I also left out batching: on a large table the single `UPDATE` holds row locks for its whole run, so backfill in chunks by primary key range instead.
